title: Musa's du'a at the well
hookLine: my Lord, I am in need of whatever good You send me (28:24)

lines: ONE BLOW, AND A MAN DEAD.
cards: Musa is running. In Egypt, he stepped into a fight to defend a man of his people, struck the other man once, and the man died. Now Pharaoh's people are looking for him.
He leaves alone, heading toward Madyan, with only a hope: maybe my Lord will guide me on the right road, he says. He arrives at a well, exhausted.
And before he does anything for himself, he notices two young women standing back from the crowd.

teach.b: Surah al-Qasas, verses twenty-three and twenty-four. A crowd of shepherds is watering their flocks. Two women hold their animals back.
Musa asks what's wrong. They say: we can't water until the shepherds have gone, and our father is a very old man. So he waters their flock for them.

Then he turns aside into the shade, and there, in Pickthall's translation, he prays: "My Lord! I am needy of whatever good Thou sendest down for me." Look how little he specifies. Not food, though he's hungry.
Not safety, though he's hunted. Not a home or a wife. Just: whatever good You send, I need it.
The Arabic word is faqir, poor, in need. And khayr, good, is left wide open. He doesn't tell Allah what the answer should look like.

teach.h: HE WATERS, THEN SITS IN THE SHADE.
teach.b: And the order: first he helps, then he sits in the shade and asks.
The answer comes in the very next verse.
One of the two women comes back, walking shyly, and says: my father invites you, to reward you for watering for us. Food, shelter, work, and later a marriage.
The Qur'an doesn't name the old father; some commentators said he was the prophet Shu'ayb, and others disagreed.
What the verses do show is how much good can arrive through one open request, prayed in the shade, by a tired man who had just helped two strangers.

how: Some Muslims say Musa's du'a (28:24) in times of need, job searches, or uncertainty, leaving the shape of the answer to Allah.

o: someone who has given everything away
a shepherd who waters other flocks
in need, open to whatever good is sent

games.q: Musa's du'a at the well — tap the pairs.

s: Musa asked Allah for a wife at the well
he asked for whatever good Allah would send, and named nothing.
the answer comes in the very next verse
28:25: one of the women returns with her father's invitation.
the Qur'an names the old father as Shu'ayb
it doesn't name him; some commentators said Shu'ayb, others disagreed.

games.q: you're Musa: hunted, exhausted, alone at a well. two women stand back with their flock. what do you do first?
games.why: he waters their flock, then turns to the shade and prays (28:23–24).

practice: Sit as if you've just come in out of the sun, into shade, and bring to mind what you need right now, noticing whether you've already decided what the answer should be. Loosen it, and hold the need open.
If you pray, say Musa's words, rabbi inni lima anzalta ilayya min khayrin faqir, my Lord, I am in need of whatever good You send me; if not, just sit with open hands.

wordCard.voice: Faqir. Poor, in need: Musa's prayer at the well, my Lord, I'm in need of whatever good You send, with nothing specified. Today's word.

orig.s: رَبِّ إِنِّي لِمَا أَنزَلْتَ إِلَيَّ مِنْ خَيْرٍ فَقِيرٌ
orig.say: RAB-bi IN-nee li-MAA an-ZAL-ta i-LAY-ya min KHAY-rin fa-QEER
orig.note: Arabic, 28:24: my Lord, I am in need of whatever good You send down to me.

carryVoice: Your line: in need of any good. First he helped, then he asked. That's six hundred ninety.
